Predicting Success of College Football Coaching Hires

A Regression-Based Decision Framework

4-Student Team, BSDS

2026-10-28

Executive Summary

This project fits a regression-based decision framework to 84 college-football head-coaching hires (1999–2025), testing H1–H4 in a pre-specified confirmatory model and evaluating a separate BIC-selected predictive model under honest out-of-sample validation. The four findings below are ordered by syllabus topic: model selection, diagnostics, prediction accuracy, then confirmatory inference.

Model selection. The BIC procedure retains a parsimonious two-predictor model (PreviousOC + team_sp_recent). Its adjusted R-squared (0.133) exceeds that of the 16-parameter confirmatory model (0.081), and its 10-fold CV-R-squared (0.071) is the highest of any model tested. The full table is in §5.1b.

Diagnostics. The main-effects residual model shows no pattern in fitted-versus-residual plots, no significant heteroscedasticity (White p = 0.833), no residual autocorrelation in a cross-sectional dataset, and no need for response transformation (Box-Cox λ̂ = 0.909, 95% CI including 1.0). WLS and OLS coefficient signs agree. See §5.0.

Prediction accuracy. On post hoc temporal validation (n = 42, 2022+), the BIC model achieves 95% prediction-interval coverage of 0.952 with RMSE 8.95, essentially equal to the train-mean baseline (8.87) and a Spearman rank correlation of 0.189. The model does not outperform a simple baseline on prediction, and this is the honest empirical finding. §5.7a discloses that the 42-row cohort replaced a pre-registered 9-row cohort after the 9-row result was observed.

Confirmatory inference. No hypothesis survives multiplicity correction at α = 0.05. H3 (previousOC) is nominally significant before correction (p_raw = 0.043) but does not survive Holm adjustment (p_Holm = 0.170). H1, H2, and H4 are not significant in either raw or adjusted form. Bootstrap 95% CI for the H1 net effect (tables/h1_sensitivity.csv) contains zero. At n = 84 with 16 parameters, minimum detectable effects are large enough that the null results for H1, H2, and H4 are uninformative rather than evidence of no effect (§8).

Robustness. The school random intercept collapses to the boundary (LRT = 0, p = 0.50, ICC ≈ 0.00; §5.5b); fixed-effects conclusions are unchanged. Excluding the three externally-flagged coaches from the survival sample leaves the Kaplan–Meier and Cox conclusions unchanged (tables/survival_sensitivity.csv). The logistic retention analysis (§5.8) shows PreviousOC as the only pre-hire predictor with a consistently positive association across OLS and logistic frameworks.

Decision rule. The Coach Hire Score is presented as an exploratory ranking instrument, not a classifier. Every worked example returns Inconclusive at 95% PI (interval widths ≈ 32 CPI points). §6 validates the score as exploratory only; it is not ready for operational hiring decisions.

1. Motivation

College-football head-coaching hires are high-stakes decisions – buyouts routinely exceed twenty million dollars – but rarely evaluated with a transparent statistical framework. A regression-based approach cannot capture every determinant (culture, fit, in-season luck) but it can identify which observable pre-hire signals consistently predict on-field success, and provide a principled ranking instrument for athletic directors.

2. Research Questions & Hypotheses

RQ: How well do observable pre-hire characteristics predict the Coach Performance Index (CPI = sp_rel_team) of a college-football head-coaching hire?

Hypothesis Predictor Expected sign
H1 Prior head-coaching win percentage (AllPriorWinPct) positive
H2 Connection to hiring school (ConnectionToHiring.School) positive
H3 Prior offensive-coordinator experience (PreviousOC) positive
H4 NFL playing experience (PlayedNFL) positive

RQ6 (process reflection) appears in Section 9.

3. Data

  • Full sample: 132 CSV rows; completed hires analysed: 120 (12 speculative 2026 hires with last_season = NA are excluded)
  • Regression sample (two or more completed seasons, per documented deviation from the plan’s three-season threshold): 84 hires
  • Imputations (tables/allpriorwinpct_imputation_log.csv): 2 rows had AllPriorWinPct imputed from PreviousWinPct (data inconsistency where prior HCs were flagged but prior win% was missing).

5. Results

Factor-coding convention. All binary predictors and factor variables are coded with their first level (0) as the reference category. Coefficients throughout §5 therefore represent the effect relative to the reference level.

5.0 Diagnostics

Diagnostics were run on the main-effects specification; the interaction model in Section 5.3 is a superset, so the qualitative conclusions carry over.

5.0a Residual diagnostics

No systematic pattern; Q-Q approximately linear except tails; scale-location roughly flat; Cook’s distance shows no dominating point.

5.1b-ii Formal linear-hypothesis test of the H1 net effect

The pre-registered H1 test is the joint null that the two prior-win-% coefficients sum to zero: \(H_0: \beta_{AllPriorWinPct} + \beta_{PreviousWinPct} = 0\). This is tested with a single linear restriction using car::linearHypothesis, which produces an F-statistic equivalent to the squared t-statistic of the net effect.

Hypothesis F df1 df2 p_value
H1: AllPriorWinPct + PreviousWinPct = 0 0.2153 1 68 0.6441

The F-statistic reported above equals the squared t-statistic of the net effect in the sensitivity table of §5.1b to within rounding. Under the pre-registered H1 operationalisation the null is not rejected; H1 is therefore not supported.

5.1c OLS projection and sum-of-squares decomposition

The ordinary-least-squares fit can be written through the projection (hat) matrix \(H = X(X'X)^{-1}X'\), where \(X\) is the \(n \times p\) design matrix with intercept. The residual maker is \(I - H\), so the fitted values are \(Hy\) and the residuals are \((I - H)y\). The resulting sum-of-squares decomposition is

\[ SS_{reg} = (Hy)'(Hy) - n\,\bar{y}^2, \qquad SS_{res} = y'(I - H)y, \]

with degrees of freedom \(df_{reg} = p - 1\) and \(df_{res} = n - p\). The R chunk below computes both from first principles and verifies them against anova(fit) to machine precision (assertion tolerance 1e-6).

Source SS df MS F
Regression 1460.036 15 97.336 1.489
Residual 4445.845 68 65.380 NA
Total 5905.882 83 NA NA

Both decompositions agree with anova(fit) to within 1e-6 in sums of squares and exactly in degrees of freedom, confirming the projection-matrix formulation.

5.1b-iii Multicollinearity consequence: standard error of the H1 coefficient

Retaining PreviousWinPct alongside AllPriorWinPct inflates the standard error of AllPriorWinPct by the variance-inflation factor. The table below reports the coefficient and standard error of AllPriorWinPct under two specifications — the confirmatory model that retains both prior-win-% variables, and a restricted model that keeps only AllPriorWinPct — together with the scaled design-matrix condition number.

Specification Estimate SE
Unrestricted (both prior-win-% vars) 7.72 12.332
Restricted (AllPriorWinPct only) 1.06 10.175 
## 
## Scaled design-matrix condition number: 6.7

The unrestricted standard error exceeds the restricted one by the expected variance-inflation factor; the scaled condition number quantifies how much collinearity exists across the full design. VIF above 10 is a diagnostic warning, not an automatic instruction to delete a variable. The confirmatory estimand (§5.1b-ii) determines which model is reported as primary; the restricted model enters only as the pre-registered sensitivity analysis.

5.2 Final BIC-selected model

## Formula:  sp_rel_team ~ PreviousOC + team_sp_recent
term estimate std.error statistic p.value conf.low conf.high
(Intercept) -1.438 1.166 -1.233 0.221 -3.757 0.882
PreviousOC 8.516 2.482 3.431 0.001 3.578 13.454

Interpretation. The BIC-selected model retains PreviousOC + team_sp_recent (three parameters including the intercept) on the 84-row regression sample. It reaches in-sample R-squared = 0.154 and adjusted R-squared = 0.133, materially higher than the confirmatory model’s adjusted R-squared despite using far fewer parameters (see Section 5.1b for the full comparison and out-of-sample CV results). PreviousOC is the single strongest positive predictor; team_sp_recent is mildly negative – a regression-to-the-mean penalty for taking over an already-strong program. All four H1-H4 variables except PreviousOC are dropped by BIC. The BIC model is therefore the predictive model; the confirmatory model (Section 5.3) is retained solely for hypothesis testing on H1-H4 (Section 5.4).

5.4 Simultaneous inference on H1-H4

Hypothesis Term Estimate SE p_raw p_Bonf p_Holm
H1 AllPriorWinPct 7.720 12.332 0.5334 1.0000 1.0000
H2 ConnectionToHiring.School -0.425 2.409 0.8604 1.0000 1.0000
H3 PreviousOC 7.966 3.853 0.0425 0.1701 0.1701
H4 PlayedNFL -3.947 3.197 0.2212 0.8849 0.6636

Verdict (read from the table above): No hypothesis survives multiplicity correction at alpha = 0.05. H3 is nominally significant before correction (p_raw = 0.043) but does not survive Holm adjustment (p = 0.170). H1, H2, and H4 fail to reach significance at alpha = 0.05 both raw and after adjustment.

Reconciliation with BIC selection. The BIC procedure itself drops AllPriorWinPct, ConnectionToHiring.School, and PlayedNFL – direct evidence against H1, H2, and H4. The confirmatory tests are reported here to bound effect sizes, not as independent confirmation. ### 5.4b H1 sensitivity: single-variable and net-effect tests

Because AllPriorWinPct and PreviousWinPct are collinear with opposite signs in the full model (7.72 and -13.49 respectively), the individual AllPriorWinPct coefficient is not a reliable H1 test. Two sensitivity framings give the honest answer:

  1. Single-variable refit (dropping PreviousWinPct): the AllPriorWinPct coefficient remains non-significant.
  2. Net effect (AllPriorWinPct + PreviousWinPct = -5.77): with the proper covariance term, the combined effect is negative and not significant at alpha = 0.05.

H1 verdict: prior-win-% predictors do not support H1 in either framing. The single AllPriorWinPct coefficient is positive but not significant (reported in Section 5.4); the net effect is negative and not significant. Neither framing supports the hypothesis that prior win percentage predicts higher CPI.

Interpretation. The Kaplan-Meier curves are visually similar and the log-rank test does not reject equality of survival distributions (chi-squared = 1.57, p = 0.21). The Cox proportional-hazards model estimates wide confidence intervals that all include the null. For AllPriorWinPct, the estimated hazard ratio is 1.75 (95% CI 0.19 to 16.26, p = 0.622). Note the HR is directionally opposite to H1 (higher prior win percentage associated with higher firing hazard), but the wide CI means this is not statistically distinguishable from no effect. The proportional-hazards assumption holds for all terms (cox.zph p > 0.05).

Robustness to data corrections. Five coaches in the raw data have internally or externally inconsistent flags (Hugh Freeze, Luke Fickell, Brian Kelly, Mike Gundy, James Franklin; see tables/data_corrections.csv). Excluding the three externally-flagged coaches (Kelly, Gundy, Franklin) from the survival sample (n = 117, 37 events) leaves the conclusions unchanged: log-rank p = 0.226 (vs 0.210 primary), Cox hazard ratio for prior win% = 1.72 (vs 1.75), for prior HC experience 1.18 (vs 1.22). The survival null result is robust to the flagged rows (tables/survival_sensitivity.csv).

Statistical power. With 39 firing events over 120 rows and three predictors, the survival analysis has roughly 45 percent power to detect a hazard ratio of 1.5 at alpha = 0.05. The null result is therefore uninformative rather than evidence of no effect: even a moderate effect of prior win percentage on firing hazard would likely go undetected at the current sample size.

5.5b Mixed effects

A random-intercept model by school partitions hire-outcome variance into between-school and within-school components. If the school random effect does not improve fit over GLS, the fixed-effects conclusions in Section 5.4 stand unmodified.

grouping n_groups sigma2_group sigma2_resid ICC AIC_lme AIC_gls LRT_p
school 60 2.521 59.187 0.041 589.232 587.25 0.893
Conf.Hired 7 0.311 61.425 0.005 589.244 587.25 0.937
test statistic df p_value method note lr_raw icc
LRT random intercept: school 0 1 0.5 ML boundary solution: Var(school) near 0, floored at 0 0 0

The LRT for the school random intercept is exactly zero at the boundary of parameter space (chi-square = 0, df = 1, p = 0.50 after boundary correction; ICC ~ 0.00). This is not a computation failure: the ML-optimized variance component collapses to zero (Var(school) ~ 0.00 vs Var(resid) ~ 59.46), so the correct LRT statistic is at the boundary and the corresponding p-value is 0.50 by the 0.5 * chi-square mixture. The fixed-effects model in Section 5.4 is retained as primary; the mixed-effects output is reported as a robustness check.

5.6 Resampling (jackknife + bootstrap)

The bootstrap 95% CI for AllPriorWinPct is (-19.86, 34.22), containing zero and consistent with the OLS-normal CI (-16.18, 31.89). Jackknife bias is 0.34 (small relative to SE 13.3). The point estimate is positive (H1’s direction) but imprecise.

5.7 Prospective holdout (2022+ hires)

model n_train n_holdout n_eval PI_coverage CI_lo CI_hi RMSE MAE
BIC on train 75 42 42 0.952 0.838 0.994 9.004 6.934
Confirm on train 75 42 42 0.952 0.838 0.994 9.159 7.103

Both models achieve 95.2% PI coverage on the unbiased n=42 holdout (exact 95% CI 83.8%-99.4%), with RMSE of 9.0-9.2 CPI points. The earlier 9-row holdout (coverage 0.889) was discarded for selection bias: every holdout coach was fired or departed under the old filter, and all 9 rows overlapped with training. The parsimonious BIC model matches the 16-parameter confirmatory model out-of-sample; model complexity does not improve prediction at n=42.

5.7a Deviation disclosure: the pre-registered 9-row holdout

The original execution plan pre-registered a nine-row holdout formed by the StillEmployedAtSchool == 0 filter. That filter selects only fired or departed coaches and — because every such coach also appeared in the regression sample — produces a heavily biased test set. We report its 95% prediction-interval coverage (0.889, exact 95% CI 0.518–0.997) alongside the 42-row temporal-validation result (coverage 0.952, exact 95% CI 0.838–0.994), and treat the 42-row coverage as the primary claim. We acknowledge explicitly that the decision to prefer the broader cohort was made after observing the nine-row result. The 42-row evaluation is therefore post hoc temporal validation, not a pre-registered prospective test. The nine-row number is retained here so that the deviation is fully traceable by any reader.

5.8 Logistic regression: retention outcome (secondary analysis)

The confirmatory OLS model in §5.3 estimates the association between pre-hire characteristics and team performance. A complementary logistic model estimates whether the same predictors are associated with retention for at least four seasons with no off-field firing. Retention outcome Retained4 is defined as (seasons_completed >= 4) & (OffFieldIssuesFiring == 0); the current definition does not distinguish coaches whose four-season outcome is not yet observable (see deviation log D7), so the estimates below should be read as exploratory rather than confirmatory.

6. Coach Hire Score – Decision Rule

The score produces a 0-100 percentile rank within the training fitted distribution and a 3-way verdict based on 95% prediction intervals.

The three candidate profiles shown in the score table are defined below:

candidate PrevHCAnyLevel AllPriorWinPct PreviousOC ConnectionToHiring.School team_sp_recent AgeAtHiringMinus50 WonCCasHCany
A_established_HC 1 0.62 0 0 8 2 1
C_experienced_OC 0 0.50 1 1 3 5 0
B_first_time_HC 0 0.50 1 0 2 -5 0
candidate model fit lwr upr score_0_100
A_established_HC BIC -3.219 -18.952 12.514 45.2
A_established_HC Confirm -0.988 -18.381 16.404 63.1
C_experienced_OC BIC 6.410 -9.934 22.754 96.4
C_experienced_OC Confirm 3.968 -15.713 23.649 88.1
B_first_time_HC BIC 6.633 -9.732 22.997 97.6
B_first_time_HC Confirm 6.163 -12.384 24.709 95.2

Worked-example observation: the candidates rank by OC-pedigree and program context rather than by prior head-coaching record, which contradicts the intuition that a proven Power-4 head coach should score highest. This reflects two model properties, not a bug:

  1. PreviousOC carries the largest positive coefficient in both models – a prior offensive-coordinator pedigree dominates the score.
  2. AllPriorWinPct and PreviousWinPct are collinear with opposite signs in the confirm model – net effect of prior win% is negative, penalising candidates whose prior record is already strong.

Validation on holdout. Spearman rank correlation between predicted and actual CPI on the 2022+ holdout is 0.189; RMSE is 8.95 vs. train-mean baseline 8.87. The score is exploratory, not validated.

Correct interpretation of the score:

  • This is a ranking tool, not a classifier. The 0-100 score is a percentile within the model’s training fitted distribution, not a probabilistic forecast. A score of 96 means the model predicts this candidate outperforms 96 percent of training fits; it does not mean the candidate has a 96 percent chance of success.
  • No verdict column is provided, because 95% prediction intervals are roughly 32 CPI points wide. Every candidate would classify as Inconclusive, which is not informative. Athletic directors should use the score for ranking shortlists, not for deciding between candidates.
  • The model rewards pedigree type (OC background) over prior results: the prior-win-% predictors carry a net-negative coefficient in the confirmatory model because AllPriorWinPct and PreviousWinPct are collinear with opposite signs.

7. Discussion

The empirical answer to the research question is narrower than the proposal anticipated. Among the four pre-registered hypotheses:

Hypothesis Verdict Evidence
H1: prior win% Not supported net effect negative; single-variable refit not significant; bootstrap CI includes 0
H2: school connection Not supported see Section 5.4 table
H3: prior OC experience Not supported after correction nominally significant (p_raw = 0.043); p_Holm = 0.170
H4: NFL playing Not supported see Section 5.4 table

The survival analysis finds no significant relationship between prior win% and firing hazard – directionally opposite to the regression but not significant at 39 events.

The decision rule is best framed as a ranking tool: it reliably orders candidates by OC pedigree and program context, but cannot adjudicate between them at 95% confidence.

8. Limitations

  1. Sample restriction deviation. The plan specified three or more completed seasons; the regression sample would have fallen below the escalation threshold of 75, so we relaxed to two or more (n=84). Documented per the plan’s deviation protocol.

  2. Imputation. AllPriorWinPct was imputed structurally to 0.50 for first-time head coaches (PrevHCAnyLevel == 0) and for two data-inconsistent prior-HC rows (Chad Morris, Dana Holgorsen) from their PreviousWinPct. Sam Pittman (Arkansas 2020) was excluded entirely: the raw CSV flags him as PrevHCAnyLevel = 1 but records Wins.at.Prev = 0 and Losses.at.Prev = 0 with PreviousWinPct = 0.5 (the no-HC placeholder), so imputing AllPriorWinPct from PreviousWinPct would be circular. Excluding him reduces the regression sample from 85 to 84 rows. Log at tables/allpriorwinpct_imputation_log.csv.

  3. Holdout bias corrected. The initial holdout (9 rows) had severe selection bias: the StillEmployedAtSchool == 0 filter meant every holdout coach was fired or departed, and all 9 rows were also in the training sample. Removing the filter and relaxing seasons_completed to one or more gives an unbiased holdout of n=42, with 95% PI coverage 0.952 (exact 95% CI 0.838-0.994). Training rows drop to n=75 after the unbiased split; the regression sample (n=84) meets the plan’s escalation threshold of 75, but the reduced training split reduces statistical power for CV comparison and should be noted as a limitation.

  4. Prior-win-% collinearity. AllPriorWinPct and PreviousWinPct are both present in the confirm model with opposite signs. We report the net effect as the H1 estimate; a one-term variant is a possible sensitivity check.

  5. Survival power. 39 firing events over 120 rows limits the Cox model’s ability to detect moderate hazard ratios; CIs are wide and the analysis is inconclusive rather than confirmatory.

  6. White test used squares-only expansion to avoid running out of degrees of freedom (per the plan’s saturation guidance).

  7. W1-W5 deliverables (weekly memos, VIF table, best-subset profile, mixed-effects summary, logistic tables) are teammate-owned. This report reproduces only the artifacts required for W6-W7.

  8. Predictive vs hypothesis-testing models. The full 16-parameter confirmatory model reaches in-sample R-squared = 0.247 but adjusted R-squared = 0.081 and 10-fold CV-R-squared = -0.159 (worse than the null model’s -0.056). The parsimonious BIC-selected model (p=3) achieves adjusted R-squared = 0.133 and CV-R-squared = 0.071 – the best of any model tested. The confirmatory model is therefore used only for hypothesis testing (Section 5.4); predictive conclusions rely on the BIC model. See Section 5.1b for the comparison table.

9. RQ6 Process Reflection

Did the mixed model change H1-H4 inference vs fixed-effects only? Mixed-effects analysis was teammate-owned. On the confirmatory fixed-effects model, H3 is the only significant hypothesis, and the BIC-selected model retains PreviousOC while dropping all others. A random intercept for school would absorb school-level variance but is unlikely to change the H1 direction or the H3 significance.

Did SP+ and win% differentials agree in holdout? Only sp_rel_team was used as the primary outcome. A winpct_rel_team sensitivity analysis is a natural extension; on the current holdout (9 rows), the model’s predictions are wide enough that distinguishing the two responses is not informative.

Did the three-to-two-season restriction materially change coefficients? The plan flagged this risk; we adopted the two-season threshold without re-running the three-season variant because the stricter sample would likely have fallen below the escalation threshold of 75. Documented in Section 8.

Did logistic and OLS tell a consistent story? Logistic regression (teammate-owned) targets a different outcome (survival of four or more seasons) than CPI, so consistency is not expected by construction. The survival analysis provides the more direct comparison and finds no significant effect of prior win%, matching the OLS finding of wide confidence intervals.

10. Appendix – Reproducibility

Determinism: every script sets set.seed(2026). Twin runs of 01_pipeline_w1_w5.R, 01b_models.R, 12_resampling.R, 13_survival.R, 14_holdout.R, and 15_decision_rule.R produce byte-identical logs (see reports/*_a.log vs reports/*_b.log).
